chapters.title: Chapter 3: Beyond VaR: Coherent Risk Measures and Backtesting

lessons.title: The Problem with VaR: Tail Risk and Non-Subadditivity

children.text: You already know VaR is silent about how bad a loss gets once you are past the threshold. This lesson goes one step further and asks a sharper question: is VaR even a well-behaved risk measure to begin with? In 1999, four academics, Artzner, Delbaen, Eber, and Heath, wrote down a short list of properties any sensible risk measure should satisfy. VaR fails one of them, and the way it fails has real, uncomfortable consequences for anyone using it to manage a diversified book.
The Four Properties of a Coherent Risk Measure

body.caption: The Artzner, Delbaen, Eber, Heath (1999) axioms for a coherent risk measure

cells: If portfolio A always loses at least as much as portfolio B in every scenario, its risk measure should be at least as high
Doubling a position size should exactly double its risk measure, no more, no less
Adding a fixed amount of risk-free cash to a portfolio should reduce its risk measure by exactly that amount
Combining two portfolios should never produce more risk than the sum of their risks separately
Not always, this is where VaR can fail

children.text: Subadditivity: Diversification Should Never Increase Risk

body.caption: Subadditivity. Holding two positions together should never be measured as riskier than the simple sum of holding them apart, this is the mathematical statement of 'diversification helps, or at worst does nothing.'

children.text: This should sound familiar. It is exactly what you saw in Chapter 2's Parametric example, where a Nifty futures position combined with gold produced a portfolio VaR lower than the sum of the two individual VaRs. That example was correctly subadditive. But that outcome depended on a specific, convenient condition: the returns involved were jointly close to normally distributed. Step outside that condition, and VaR's good behavior is not guaranteed.
A Concrete Counterexample: When VaR Breaks Its Own Logic

This is a hypothetical, illustrative example, not a real issuer. A fund holds two Rs 10,00,000 corporate NCDs, issued by two unrelated companies, Company A and Company B. Each bond independently has a 4% one-year default probability, and for simplicity assume zero recovery on default, the entire principal is lost. Neither bond has any other source of return volatility in this simplified example.

body.caption: Outcome distribution for each bond, held alone

body.text: For either bond held alone, the 95% VaR asks: what loss threshold is exceeded no more than 5% of the time? Since the probability of any loss at all is only 4%, which is below the 5% threshold, the 95th percentile outcome is simply zero loss. VaR at 95% for Bond A alone is Rs 0. Same for Bond B alone.

children.text: Now combine both bonds in one portfolio, assuming their defaults are independent of each other.

body.caption: Outcome distribution for the combined two-bond portfolio

stats.label: VaR 95%, combined portfolio
stats.context: P(loss > 0) = 7.84%, above 5%, so the threshold moves up to the next outcome

body.text: VaR(Bond A) plus VaR(Bond B) equals Rs 0 plus Rs 0, which is Rs 0. VaR(combined portfolio) is Rs 10,00,000. That means VaR(A+B) is greater than VaR(A) plus VaR(B), the exact opposite of subadditivity. By this measure, holding both bonds together looks riskier than holding either one alone, even though diversifying across two independent, unrelated issuers is, in every real economic sense, the safer choice. VaR does not merely understate risk here, it points a fund manager in the wrong direction if used mechanically to compare a concentrated position against a diversified one.

children.text: When Does VaR Actually Behave Well?

VaR is provably subadditive when the returns involved are jointly normally distributed, or more generally, elliptically distributed, a broader family of symmetric, well-behaved distributions that includes the normal. That is precisely the condition under which Chapter 2's Nifty-and-gold example worked out cleanly. The failure shows up specifically with skewed, discontinuous, or binary-style payoffs, exactly what a default event, a knock-in barrier, or a deep out-of-the-money option position looks like.

body.title: When VaR's Diversification Logic Is Safe vs When It Can Break

columns.label: Generally Safe
points: Portfolios of linear positions with roughly normal or elliptical joint returns
Large, well-diversified equity and futures books without heavy credit or default exposure
The kind of Parametric VaR example worked through in Chapter 2

columns.label: Can Break Down
points: Credit and default risk, bonds, NCDs, counterparty exposure with low-probability, high-severity outcomes
Portfolios with deep out-of-the-money options or other binary-style payoffs
Any situation where the underlying risk is sharply skewed rather than roughly symmetric

body.title: Reproduce the Non-Subadditivity Result
body.prompt: Two independent bonds, Rs 5,00,000 principal each, each with a 3% one-year default probability and zero recovery on default. Using 95% confidence, what is the VaR of the combined two-bond portfolio, in rupees?
body.explanation: P(neither defaults) = 0.97 squared = 94.09%. P(loss > 0) = 5.91%, which is above the 5% threshold, so the 95% VaR is not Rs 0. P(both default) = 0.09%, well under 5%, so the threshold settles at the one-default outcome: Rs 5,00,000. Since each bond alone has only a 3% default probability, below the 5% cutoff, each individual VaR is Rs 0, reproducing the same non-subadditive result as the worked example.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why does combining the two independent bonds increase the 95% VaR, when combining two normally distributed assets in Chapter 2 decreased it?
options: Because bonds always have higher volatility than equities
Because default risk is a low-probability, discontinuous outcome, which pushes the combined portfolio's probability of any loss above the 5% cutoff, while each bond alone stays just under it
Because the calculation in Chapter 2 was done incorrectly
Because 95% confidence is too low to use for bonds
body.explanation: The Chapter 2 example involved roughly normally distributed, continuous returns, where VaR's subadditivity holds. Here, each bond's loss event is rare enough on its own to fall below the 5% VaR cutoff, but combining two such independent low-probability events raises the probability of at least one loss above that same cutoff, flipping the VaR comparison.

body.text: VaR can tell you, incorrectly, that diversification made you riskier. A risk measure that can get diversification backwards is not fully trustworthy for portfolio decisions, no matter how precisely it is calculated.

points: A coherent risk measure satisfies monotonicity, positive homogeneity, translation invariance, and subadditivity. VaR satisfies the first three but can fail the fourth.
Subadditivity means combining two positions should never look riskier than holding them separately. VaR is provably subadditive under normal or elliptical joint distributions.

With skewed, discontinuous, low-probability-high-severity risks like default or deep out-of-the-money options, VaR can violate subadditivity, making a diversified position appear riskier than a concentrated one.
The worked bond example showed VaR(A) = VaR(B) = Rs 0 individually, but VaR(A+B) = Rs 10,00,000 combined, a direct, quantified violation of diversification logic.
This is exactly the gap Expected Shortfall, covered in the next lesson, was built to close, it is a coherent risk measure by construction and does not suffer from this failure mode.
